segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we've seen how me can mean me, to me, or myself. And te can mean you, to you, or yourself. And nos can mean us, to us, or ourselves. So we want to resist the temptation to translate this "to". So for example, he speaks to me...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: ...we don't need this "to" because me, me, can mean me, to me, or myself. So we want to resist the temptation to translate that "to". So how do you say he speaks to me, or he is speaking to me?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Habla me. Oh sorry, me habla.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yeah, don't let that "to" confuse you about the position it should go. It's still going before. Me habla. They speak to me?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. If you want to say they speak to me about it, you can just say they speak me it, in Spanish.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Me lo hablan. Very good. They're speaking to me about it. So this "to" and this "about", we notice Spanish tends not to need these words as much as English does.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: For example, to buy was comprar. Comprar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So this me other than to me can be for me, from me. We don't really need these words. So for example, if you want to say he buys it for me, we can just say he buys me it. So comprar is to buy. He buys it for me. He buys me it.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Me lo compra. So here we see me is like "for me" here, but it's just me, we're just using me. I buy it for you, speaking informally. I buy it for you.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now if you want to say shall I buy it for you? "Shall" in English, all it's doing really is just making it a question. Shall I buy it for you? So in Spanish just make it sound like a question.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yeah. ¿Te lo compro? Shall I buy it for you? Now this could actually even mean from you. Shall I buy it from you? So by the context we'll understand the difference.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Maybe you will hear if you travel to a Spanish-speaking country people saying "buy me", selling things in the street. "Buy me something" is what you will hear. And they're probably not asking you to buy them something, but to buy something from them. And it's understood and we don't really need to use these words like "from" or "for" most of the time.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: To do was hacer. Hacer. How would you say do you want to do, speaking informally?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Doesn't matter, does it? Do you want to do?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Do you want to do it?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. ¿Quieres hacerlo? Now how do you think you would say do you want to do it for me?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yes. ¿Me lo quieres hacer? So we're not using the word for "for", we don't need it in Spanish. It's understood. Do you want to do it for me? ¿Me lo quieres hacer? ¿Quieres hacérmelo? Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: The kitchen in Spanish is la cocina. La cocina, or in most of Spain, la cocina, cocina. La cocina.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And to cook is cocinar. You just make a verb from cocina. Cocinar. Actually this is where we get concoction, concoction, from, in English with cooking. So how would you say I cook from cocinar?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. How do you say he cooks, or she cooks, or it cooks, or usted, you formal cook?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. And with emphasis or clarification, if you want to use the word for you?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Tú cocinas. Good. They cook, or you guys?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. What if we wanted to use the word for they to emphasize or to clarify?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Ellos cocinan. Good. Or ellas if it's a female group. What if we wanted to say you guys are cooking, with the emphasis or the clarification?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Ustedes cocinan. And we cook, what is we cook?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. And with the emphasis or the clarification?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Nosotros cocinamos. Good. How would you say I can? How is I can related to power?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Puede. And you can, informal?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Can you cook something for me? So what was the word for something?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. How do you think you're going to say this in Spanish? Can you cook something for me?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. ¿Me puedes cocinar algo? ¿Puedes cocinarme algo? Either way. So how would you say I have cooked? I have cooked.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we said that this this tense of have cooked, I have cooked, instead of I cooked, we can use it more in Spanish than in English. So for example in English it sounds much more natural to say I cooked at six o'clock. But in Spanish it's not a problem to say I have cooked at six o'clock.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, at six o'clock is a las seis. What you actually mean when you say a las seis is a las seis horas, at the six hours. A little bit like in English when you say at 1600 hours. A las seis. So how would you say I have cooked at six o'clock, I cooked at six o'clock?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. He cocinado a las seis. I have cooked at six o'clock. I cooked at six o'clock. Good. The word for eight in Spanish is ocho. Ocho.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Ocho. We have this similar root in octagon, you know a shape with eight sides, or octopus, which has eight legs, or in October, which although now it's the 10th month, in the Roman calendar there were only 10 months and October was month number eight. So ocho, eight. How would you say we have cooked at eight o'clock? We have cooked at eight o'clock.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Hemos cocinado a las ocho. The word for nine in Spanish is nueve.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Nueve. We can see in November, which used to be the ninth month, the o splits into ue, nueve. And we have the same with 10. 10 is diez or diez in most of Spain, diez. What does that sound like if we go back to our calendar?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: December, which used to be the 10th month. And of course again an example of splitting, dec to diez.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Quedar, in Spanish quedar, means to remain or to to be left over, and it actually has quite a few other meanings as well. It's quite a flexible verb, quedar. But for now, to remain or to be left over. Q-u-e-d-a-r, quedar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And qu in Spanish is always a k sound. You must resist any temptation to pronounce "quedar" if you were to read this. The word que, the word for what, that we learned to spell q-u-e, quiero is spelt q-u-i-e-r-o, so qu this combination is always a k. Quedar means to remain.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So in Spanish if you want to say I stay, actually you say I remain myself. This is the way you say I stay in Spanish. So we start with remain, which is quedar. So how do you say I remain?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: The e doesn't split here, but good for trying.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Me quedo. This means I stay. Me quedo. Until until in Spanish is hasta. Hasta. H-a-s-t-a. You may have heard hasta la vista, until the view, literally until the seeing, until we see each other. Hasta la vista.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So now you can say I'm staying here until 10:00. So let's divide it up. I'm staying here, I remain myself here...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yes, las diez. Yeah, it's literally like las diez horas, but you don't say horas. Maybe historically people said it, but not anymore. Me quedo aquí, or acá, hasta las diez. Good. I'm staying until 10:00.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So if me quedo, I remain myself, is I'm staying, how do you think you would say we are staying?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good, but now you have some vowel harmony popping in because we were concentrating on on the other bit, so this mistake managed to come back.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good, because it's quedar, no? Nos quedamos. We remain ourselves, we stay. So, we're staying until 9:00?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Nos quedamos hasta las nueve. Very good. Very good. You stay, or you remain yourself, speaking informally?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Te quedas. You're staying here?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Te quedas aquí. Are you staying here?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. ¿Te quedas aquí? How would you make it emphatic now, are you staying here? Because this te is not emphatic, it's not optional. We have to put this me in me quedo to get the meaning of stay, and we have to put this te in te quedas to get the meaning of stay. But if we want to make it emphatic, what do we add?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Yo me quedo. Good. We're staying?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Nos quedamos. Good. We are staying?
